utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters. I hope that the day together is going to be good. Also, good morning to Defence counsel, to the accused. They say that one finds solutions over the night, so who is the witness now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Apparently, we're going to have Mr. Tadic. Mr. Tadic will be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. First, let me thank the Defence, and I'm sure that it was the Defence that convinced Mr. Tadic to remain here, and the two of us would like to thank Mr. Tadic as well. I know that it wasn't easy for him, it might have caused him some problems, but having said this, we can have Mr. Tadic brought into the courtroom now. The Prosecution still has 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you have 30 minutes. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, please be seated. You're still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, on behalf of myself and Judge Shahabuddeen, I would like to thank you for having remained available to the Tribunal. I know that it was difficult for you. I know that you have a busy schedule, and you have shown a great deal of patience. We are all available and at the disposal of justice with a big "J." I think, however, that you will be able to leave today. I hope so. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Once again, I would like to thank the Defence counsel. Mr. Harmon, you have until about a quarter to eleven to finish your cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Judge Shahabuddeen, and good morning, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Harmon: (Cont'd)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tadic, and welcome, once again, to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, yesterday we were talking about an order given by Colonel Blaskic on May 10th to SIS to conduct an investigation. In the course of that testimony, you said that you believed that SIS was part of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me show you Defence Exhibit 167, and I have taken the liberty, Counsel, so you know, to take my copy of 167 and highlight it, and we will put my copy, if that is agreeable, on the ELMO to show Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, this is an exhibit that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is the exhibit? I don't think that the Defence knows what the exhibit is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's 167. It is the organogram introduced by counsel in his opening statement showing the structure of Herceg-Bosna, so if we could have that placed on the ELMO --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President, but if it's been altered or highlighted, then it's no longer D167. It's a new document with new characteristics. It should be marked, and we have no objection to counsel using it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to get hypertechnical. Mr. Hayman has marked plenty of exhibits in the course of this trial. We're using this for illustration. Mr. Dubuisson has confirmed that what has been shown to him by the assistant is, in fact, a copy of Defence Exhibit 167, with the exception of two colours, the colour yellow and the colour green, that have been placed on this exhibit. Is that correct, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. After having checked it, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. You have the guarantee of the registrar, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's just that it's a new exhibit if it's been marked, Your Honour. That's all. If we mark on somebody else's exhibits, we mark it as a new exhibit so there's a record of what the witness is being shown. We need a record in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is to save time and so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Harmon, would you agree to our giving it another number so that we can begin the day without entering into sterile discussions? Mr. Hayman, first of all, let me ask you if you're satisfied if we give it another number, since it now has yellow and green on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine, Mr. President. I'm happy to give it another number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson, since colours are very important, we all know that. There are colours on flags, there are colours in different clans, and also colours for exhibits. All right. That's the end of this incident. Mr. Registrar, would you give us a new number for that exhibit, which will be 167 but with colours? There's a black and white version and a colour version, like in the movies. All right. We can give it a new number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be 569.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I'd like to show you Prosecutor's 569, which is an identical copy of Defence Exhibit 167 that was introduced by Mr. Hayman in his opening statement. Let me direct your attention to the colours. Yesterday, you said that the SIS was part of the military police, and let me direct your attention, first of all, to the yellow colours. If you go to the bottom box marked in yellow, you will see that the SIS for Central Bosnia is in that particular box, and if you follow the line of command up, you will see that they answered to the head office for security and information service which then, in turn, answered to the department of defence. Now, a separate chain of command existed, according to this document, for the military police, and if we could start, Mr. Tadic, I'll orient you with the green box on the bottom indicating the 4th Military Police Battalion, and it is and should be connected with the three boxes above that which are the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Military Police Battalion, all of which answered to the head office for military police which, in turn, answered to the department of defence. So when you said that SIS was part of the military police, is this diagram correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know the date of this diagram, which period it refers to. Second, I said, as far as I can recall, and we can check that in the transcript, that I think that for a time, it was in the composition of the military police, and if you want me to say why I think this and why I know that was that in 1992, in the summer, I was present, and I'll be quite frank, to a quarrel that went on in Mostar as to whether SIS and the military police should remain together. When they separated, how matters proceeded after that, I did not follow this fact afterwards because it did not come within my domain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On May the 10th, 1993, to your knowledge, was SIS part of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in a normal investigation, the competency to investigate criminal conduct was under the investigative section of the military police; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we'll leave that subject for a moment, and let me turn to a new topic, and that is, within the rules and laws and regulations that you have testified about before this Court, who had the power to appoint the head of a military police battalion?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: To be quite frank with you, I did not study that. I can only give you a hypothetical answer, but not with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you give us that answer, please?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I cannot tell you with any certainty who had that power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Colonel Blaskic have the power to appoint the head of the 4th Military Police Battalion in the Central Bosnia Operations Zone?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know that. One would have to study the acts and documents and see what the competencies were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me now turn to a different topic, and that is, Mr. Tadic, did Colonel Blaskic have the power and authority under the laws and rules which you've testified about to give commands to the civilian HVO police?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The civilian police, no, because it had its own interior affairs department in 1992 and 1993. It had its own setup, and at the head of it was the head of the department for the interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/5 and 456/38. Mr. Tadic, you have been given a copy of -- let me see which document it is. You've been given a copy of 456/5, and you will see in examining that document, Mr. Tadic, that this document is dated the 31st of December, 1992, and it is directed to, among others, the chief of the Travnik department. I'd like to draw your attention -- let me just make one other clarification on this. This is an order that was issued by Colonel Blaskic, as you can see. Now, directing your attention to the first paragraph in that, you will see that Colonel Blaskic assigns three civilian police officers and one military police officer to a particular checkpoint. He gives an order to the civilian police to perform certain duties, and in paragraph 3 of that particular document, that order, you will see that Colonel Blaskic tells the police officers what they have to do, that is, check civilians, humanitarian aid convoys, et cetera. If you would refer to paragraph 7 of that document, Mr. Tadic, you will see that Colonel Blaskic orders that the chief of the police department select persons to be assigned to the checkpoint and requires that the chief of police inform him in writing by the 3rd of January, 1993, and he gives, in paragraph 9, a date of compliance with that particular order. Now, let me show you the next exhibit, Mr. Tadic, which is 456/38 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecutor did not give the witness enough time to peruse the document. He has passed through the document very quickly because he knows it, whereas the witness needs time to read through the document if we wish to have a good quality answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no problem. I'm trying to facilitate the speed of this examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is a Prosecution document. It's absolutely legitimate for the Prosecution to show exhibits about which the witness has to react. If the witness can't react to them, he can tell us, but please, let the witness answer, please. If the witness needs a little bit of time in order to familiarise himself with the document, of course, we can give him the time, so long as it's not too long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you satisfied, Mr. Tadic, that you have had enough time to review 456/5, and have I accurately described the contents of those numbered provisions which I referred to?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said yesterday already that I did not have an opportunity to see any of these documents which were given to me yesterday and today by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said yesterday that none of the documents that were shown to me yesterday and that I see here now again today, I have not seen these before; however, I can give my opinion, which is, of course, my vision of the contents of these documents, and the Court will decide and assess that. Under the competence of the commander was what we called a daily use, operative daily use, of the military police and, amongst other things, the regulation of traffic. When we're talking about the civilian police, it had its own setup, it had its own department, and at that time, that is to say, the date, the 31st of December, 1992, it was not the ministry, but it was a department. It would be natural, I say it would be natural, that is my legal viewpoint, to go to the commander of the civilian police and then the two police forces to act in a coordinated fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, this is an order to the civilian police to perform certain tasks, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In paragraph 7, the civilian and military police and the head of the 4th Battalion, so both civilian and military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/38. This is a document, as you will see, that has been issued by Colonel Blaskic, and it is directed to, among others, the commander of the police station in Vitez. It's an order. If you will direct your attention to certain provisions. I would like you to peruse the document in total. It's a short document, but this is an order to provide unobstructed passage for the convoy of food to the village of Krusica on the 21st of June, 1993. And, as you see in paragraph 5, Colonel Blaskic says that, "I shall hold the commanders of --" and he goes on to identify certain groups, "-- the Vitez police station responsible for ensuring compliance with this order." So, Mr. Tadic, this is another order by Colonel Blaskic to the civilian police in which Colonel Blaskic as the operation zone commander holds the civilian police chief, or the civilian police commander personally responsible to him, the military commander of the Operative Zone. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but here there are four orders, in fact, towards the brigade, which he has the right to do, towards the military police, which he once again has the right to do, and one of them is towards the civilian police. So paragraph 5 includes four, that is to say there are four subjects in paragraph 5. Why he did this, why Mr. Blaskic did this, vis-a-vis the civilian police, he can give you, I suppose, an answer to that. But I have given you a precise answer and I cannot express his desires.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I am not asking you for Colonel Blaskic's desires. I am asking you to comment on this document. You've come here as a witness to testify about the laws and the rules and the regulations that existed in Herceg-Bosna during the relevant period of time. This is an order by Colonel Blaskic to the commander of the civilian police department in Vitez where the military zone commander personally holds responsible the civilian police chief. My question to you, Mr. Tadic, is what was his legal authority to do that?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I have already said, he should not have, and he could not have acted that way, but this is a cumulative order. That is to say, it is towards four individuals, not only the head of the civilian police. That is one of four. I said earlier on that he should have followed the road of the civilian police organisation and set-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So he was acting outside of his competencies when he gave that order to the civilian police chief, correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me turn your attention to another topic, and that is the topic of prisons. Your testimony two days ago, which is found at page 57, lines 3 through 7, you were asked a question by my colleague, Mr. Nobilo, and the question was as follows: "Did Blaskic, according to any basis, was he authorised to control or command what was happening in a military detention centre or a military prison?" And your answer was: "No, that was not his competence or authority." So what you are telling this Court is Colonel Blaskic couldn't order wardens of military detention facilities what to do. Do I understand your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me show you Defence Exhibit 373, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that you have to finish at a quarter to 11.00. Please don't forget. About a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, take a look at that document, please, Mr. Tadic. This is a command, you will see that it is issued to wardens of military prisons, it was issued on the 21st of June, 1993, and it was issued by Colonel Blaskic. Now, this is a command, as you can see, in respect of the regulations of the Geneva Conventions. You will see that Colonel Blaskic, according to this Defence Exhibit, is commanding certain conduct not take place within the military prisons. And, as you will see in paragraph 4, Colonel Blaskic says, "I hold responsible brigade commanders and wardens of military prisons for carrying out this order." Tell me, please, Mr. Tadic, what was Colonel Blaskic's legal authority to hold responsible a warden of a military prison?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Blaskic did not have competencies towards military prisons. That is clearly stated in the regulation relating to district military courts and other documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question, then: He had an obligation under the Geneva Conventions to ensure that those conventions were complied with; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If in fact Colonel Blaskic was aware that there were violations of these conventions that were taking place within his operation zone as a military commander, he had a paramount obligation to ensure that those violations were taken care of, were corrected, were ameliorated; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That should have been done by every commander, including Commander Blaskic, but within the regulations that envisages this, that is to say what the courts do. The courts are responsible for their work, prisons, civilian prisons and within their frameworks they had military departments, military units, and they had their commanders. The civilian section had a civilian chief and the military had a military chief. The defence department, therefore, had supervision over this, and Blaskic should have, legally speaking of course, I am saying what I would do as a legal man, should have written a letter to the defence department and telling them that he has the knowledge that such and such actions are not in keeping with the conventions, will you take the necessary steps, please, a letter to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what we are talking about are military prisons and detention facilities that are recognised, that are identified as a military prison, for example, the Kaonik military prison, correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Kaonik, I am telling you now, we didn't have purely military prisons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Kaonik, according the regulations, was one of the civilian prisons which had a military prison unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, Mr. Tadic, in respect of locations where prisoners of war and civilians were detained that were not official military prisons; for example, a command headquarters; for example, a school or a chess club. Under those circumstances whose obligation was it to ensure that the prisoners of war and the civilians were being accorded the proper treatment under the Geneva Conventions and the other international conventions?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The regulations, the rules and regulations state that with regard to prisoners of war, it is the military police who is in charge, which is in charge of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about detained civilians?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: And civilians. In any case, everything that is not under the courts treatment, so-to-speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What obligation in the operation zone of Central Bosnia did Colonel Blaskic have vis-a-vis those detained civilians and prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what -- of course, he would have to see that the conventions were respected, but there were services working in this regard, that is to say the military police controlling facilities of this kind, where civilians were detained or prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I only have a few minutes left. Let me turn to a different topic. When you testified about the rules and regulations, Mr. Tadic, that affected the district military courts and the district military prosecutor and the military police, your testimony didn't mean to imply that Blaskic didn't have the power to control and punish his subordinates, because there was a separate set of regulations, the rules of military discipline that you did not testify about. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's turn our attention and the Court's attention to the rules of military discipline, and the powers that Colonel Blaskic had under those particular rules. I see Mr. Nobilo is up, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My learned colleague has just said that Mr. Tadic did not testify about the disciplinary rules and regulations, so if he did not testify on this in the examination-in-chief, he cannot do it during the cross-examination, because it is outside the focus of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, yesterday Mr. Tadic did refer to the rules of military discipline in response to a question that I raised. I think, in terms of pure fairness, and so that the Court is not misguided or left with an impression that Colonel Blaskic had very, very limited powers in respect to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ask your question, Mr. Harmon. Ask your question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please, Mr. Tadic, you are familiar with the rules of military discipline, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No. I only know that they exist, but I didn't study them. It had nothing to do with my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen them?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I mean, I saw it as a document, but I didn't read all of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you gave us testimony at great length about how evidence is gathered by the military police, how it goes to a military district prosecutor and how it goes to a military district court. Are you aware, Mr. Tadic, that there was also, at the same time, a parallel system of discipline that Colonel Blaskic could impose on an offender?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that the part related to the law on criminal procedure was involved because it was applied by the crime investigation military police, and that is what the rules clearly say. As far as discipline is concerned, and the rules of discipline, as a lawyer, as a citizen, as a legal person who was always involved in certain segments, I know that the commander does have certain authority. After all, I was a soldier before the war, and I know that a commander can take certain disciplinary action. As far as I remember, the maximum prison sentence was 60 days. I did not study the rules or regulations involved. I do know that it was the military police that took care of these persons who were punished in a disciplinary sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I see Prosecutor's Exhibit 38, please, and ask that that be shown to Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Is this a Defence or a Prosecution -- all right. Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tadic, what has been placed in front of you should be the rules of military discipline. Do you have those in front of you, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were promulgated in September of 1992. Now, let me ask you some questions, because you were a soldier and you are a lawyer and you were the Minister of Defence -- Minister of Justice, I'm sorry. Let me ask you to refer to Article 3 of that particular set of rules. Do you see Article 3?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That indicates, does it not, and are you familiar with this provision, that any act of military personnel that contravenes the rules of military discipline and orders issued by superior officers should be considered a breach of military discipline? And under paragraph 8, a breach of military discipline includes all other illegal acts that are damaging to the reputation of the armed forces. Are you familiar with that provision?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the first time I see it. The norm that you just presented to me is one I see for the first time, because I was not involved in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me direct your attention, sir, to Article 29 of this particular set of rules and regulations. I would like to direct your attention to the first paragraph, because this impinges somewhat on your testimony the other day. Article 29 in the first paragraph says: "That when an authorised officer establishes that a breach of military discipline is also a punishable act, the case shall be handed to an authorised prosecutor through official channels." Now, I want to read the second sentence, because we come to the second prong of this: "If it is in the interest of the service, the officer shall also undertake measures to initiate disciplinary proceedings." So there can be a dual track of sanctions. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the military disciplinary courts where military discipline was imposed are separate and distinct from the military district courts, correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The military disciplinary prosecutors are separate and distinct from the district military prosecutors, correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic did not have the authority or competency to appoint the district military prosecutor, but he did have the authority to appoint the military disciplinary prosecutor. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The district military prosecutor, no. He did not have that authority, and it says quite clearly in the decree who appoints the prosecutor. But as far as the military disciplinary prosecutor is concerned, I told you a few minutes ago that I have not read this document. But it is certain that it was regulated, I mean, who appoints the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Tadic, there may have been a translation error. I didn't say Colonel Blaskic had the power to appoint a district military prosecutor. I said he had the power and authority to appoint a disciplinary court prosecutor. And your answer, I understood, you are not familiar with that document. Let me turn to a different part of this and refer you, please --

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- very briefly, Mr. Tadic, to Articles 10 and 11 which discuss the punishments that are available for a disciplinary error or a disciplinary offence. You will see in there, in respect of disciplinary errors, which are minor offences, that the sanctions include anything from a warning to a military detention of up to 30 days. Now, in respect of disciplinary offences, the disciplinary punishments can include suspension, pay cuts, discharge from active service, and detention for up to 30 days and other sanctions. I've only named some of them. Am I correct, Mr. Tadic, from your review of that particular Rule?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me direct your attention to Article 60 of this particular document. Again, we are dealing with the military disciplinary system and not the legal system that you described. That in Article 60 -- actually, in Article 59, as soon as a military superior officer learns of a breach of discipline, he is obligated under Article 59 to undertake all necessary measures to secure evidence and collect information that's relevant to establishing the facts of the offence. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under Article 60 of this particular provision it indicates under the second paragraph: "Disciplinary investigation of non-commissioned officers and officers appointed to state administrative agencies, enterprises and other legal entities shall be initiated by a decision of an officer holding the post of commander of the Operative Zone." So the decision to initiate an investigation falls on the shoulders of the commander of the Operative Zone under this provision, correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Article 60, just like the entire rules, pertains to these disciplinary measures, and Article 60 says quite clearly disciplinary action against non-commissioned officers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what we are talking about, disciplinary actions, Mr. Tadic. I am not talking about district military courts or district military prosecutors, I am talking about this regulatory scheme dealing with discipline within the HVO. So let's be clear on that. Now, disciplinary investigation of non-commissioned officers and officers of the armed forces shall be initiated by a decision of an officer holding the post of brigade commander and a corresponding or higher post. That's in the first provision. So Blaskic could initiate a disciplinary action under this set of rules, likewise a brigade commander could initiate an action for disciplinary action, correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never said otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me move on, Mr. Tadic. Mr. Tadic, let me move on very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting counsel. If there was something being added to the documents here, that's one thing, but counsel is simply reading the documents. The witness hasn't had anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am waiting for the interpretation. Yes. Yes, that's correct. Counsel is reading the documents. The witness has to be able to give his opinion. You are right, Mr. Hayman. Mr. Harmon, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a long way of getting to my question, because it relates to the witness's testimony, but I need to lay some predicate questions first. And if I can just get through a few more questions, Mr. President, I will rapidly come to a close of this examination. So if I, with the Court's indulgence, can ask some additional questions. I have my eye on the clock. I am moving as fast as I can. Mr. Nobilo once again wants some of my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Don't take too much time from the Prosecution, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I won't. One minute. In principle, I think that this line of questioning is wrong. Mr. Tadic said that he did not see this document, that he never worked on this particular piece of work, he was not involved in discipline. He cannot give any kind of answer. He can only listen to the Prosecutor reading out documents. I don't see any sense in this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, you are not Mr. Tadic's lawyer. He has a lawyer. He is familiar with the rules. He was a minister himself. Let Mr. Harmon do his work. Let him ask the question. If Mr. Tadic doesn't know, he will say he doesn't know, but we are dealing with his area of competence. If he says he is not familiar with these regulations, it would be normal for the Prosecutor to familiarise him with it. We are wasting time. That was a minute for Mr. Nobilo and a minute for Jorda. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, let me direct your attention to Article 67. That indicates that the decision to bring the offender before the military disciplinary court shall be issued by, one, the commander of the armed forces or, two, the commander of the Operative Zone for non-commissioned officers and officers up to the rank of brigadier serving in the units or institutions which are subordinate to the Operative Zone commander. The decision to bring the offender to a military disciplinary court rested on Colonel Blaskic's shoulders, according to this provision, did it not, as well as the commander of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Take time to think about it, Mr. Tadic. It's an important question. We are at the very heart of an important issue. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, you put it very nicely a few minutes ago. Yes, I am a lawyer, yes I have been involved in legal matters for a long time. I was not involved in military matters. The Prosecutor read this to me, and he read it the way he read it, and what else can I answer? If I were to be involved in the entire subject matter, I would have to read out the entire rules and regulations, because you know how dangerous it is to take out only one provision out of a law or a legal document. It has to be interpreted within the context of the entire rules and regulations and, therefore, I cannot say anything else but that is what it says here. That is what it says here. I don't know whether there is another norm which translates this norm in relative terms. I do not know that because I never read these rules and regulations, because I did not need it for my own line of work. I think that that is the way this should be perceived. I should not be put in a position to speak because I am a lawyer about this, because if any legal person wants to speak competently, he has to study the material in its entirety. Then it is not going to be a partial answer, but one in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying, Mr. Tadic, but the question, afterall, was not that complicated as it appears. You can always answer that you need a few days to familiarise yourself with all the rules, but it does seem to me that it's a relatively easy question. All you have to do is to read Articles 59 and 60. These are not very complicated articles. That's all I want to say. But if you don't know, then you don't, and it will be noted that Mr. Tadic is not familiar with the regulations of the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, let me come back to the question I asked you a moment ago. Under Article 67, the decision to bring the offender before a military disciplinary court shall be issued by the commander of the armed forces under provision 1, or under provision 2, the commander of the Operative Zone for non-commissioned officers and officers up to the rank of brigadier serving, they were subordinate to him in the Operative Zone, correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that is a provision which says exactly what you read out. Again, I say is there another provision that relativises (sic) it? That I don't know because I never studied this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to two exhibits very quickly, 456/69, 68 and 69. These exhibits, just to give you a preview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, do you have an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we were plowing some new ground, we don't want to cut off the Prosecutor, but the Prosecutor, for 10, 15 minutes now, he has been reading documents that, one, speak for themselves and, two, this witness has no particular expertise. We are wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, I would note, Mr. Hayman, that you yourself state that they are self-evident. That's important. It's self-evident documents. I also remind the Prosecutor of his time constraints. You can't ask the witness and -- well, there has to be a certain equity in these discussions. I do this with the agreement of Judge Shahabuddeen, that is we try to be flexible, because the Judges are also interested in everything that's being said, and that's natural. But having said that, Mr. Harmon, you cannot really go through all of these areas. You've got to establish priorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have three more areas of this document to go through and then I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I have to ask you how many more minutes do you need? Otherwise I am going to be somewhat dictatorial. I want this trial to be conducted in a proper amount of time. How many more moments do you need in order to finish what you are doing, and after that I am going to interrupt? It's the rule. It's the rule of equity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Without interruption, Mr. President, I will be concluded in ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. This is your procedure, Mr. Harmon. This is part of the procedure, but I cannot refuse the right of someone to make an objection. Mr. Harmon, I'm going to give you five minutes, and after that, we have to stop. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I appreciate that. I will accept the Court's decision. I will withdraw those exhibits. I will merely direct Your Honours' attention to those exhibits which are 456/68 and 466/69 which are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. You never use that procedure. You always think that you're dealing with unprofessional Judges. Provide the documents, the exhibits. I have not applied the new Rules of Procedure and Evidence because these rules were set into place and the trial had begun in 1997, but the spirit of the new rules is the following: Trust the Judges, provide them with documents, provide them with briefs, so that we can speed things up; otherwise, we will be here for another three years. You can tell us what it is you want to draw our attention to, and then in your closing arguments, you can develop your arguments. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. I will adopt the procedure out of necessity, and let me direct Your Honours' attention to Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/69 and 456/70, which are two orders by Colonel Blaskic where he identifies the powers that he has in him pursuant to Article 12, Article 22, and Article 31 of the military disciplinary manual to impose sentences, and you will see in 456/69 and 456/70, Colonel Blaskic sentences one individual to 60 days and another individual in a different order to 30 days. I would also direct Your Honours' attention to Article 94 of the rules of military discipline and Article 95, because these are articles which show the extent to which Colonel Blaskic had control over the military disciplinary courts. Article 94 indicates, and I will read it: "The commander of the unit or institutions where the military disciplinary courts shall supervise the work of the military disciplinary courts and their prosecutors." I direct your attention to Article 95 as well. Article 95 indicates as follows: "The president of the first instance military disciplinary court and the prosecutor shall bear disciplinary liability for their work in court --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're quoting the text. That's enough. The Judges will read it themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you have a final question regarding all of the powers, all of the powers that you believe that the accused had? If you do, please ask it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tadic, it's fair to say that in respect of the rules of military discipline, Colonel Blaskic had considerably more powers at his disposal than the powers you described he had under the rules relating to the military district prosecutor and the military district courts; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you testified at page 16 in your testimony, and I will read the question to you by Mr. Nobilo and your answer or part of your answer: "Tell me, according to your interpretations and your perception of the work of military courts, the commander of an operative zone, in this specific case, Colonel Blaskic, who was subordinated to the main staff, did he have anything to do with the establishment of the courts, the appointment of judges, the control over the work of courts or military prosecutors' offices, and the like," and your answer was, "No, no. It is the defence department that had this right." When you gave that particular answer, you weren't referring to the military disciplinary courts, were you?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not to the disciplinary courts but to the courts that were established by way of the decree on district military courts that we elaborated on and where it says explicitly who appoints judges and who they are accountable to, who they submit reports to, and who supervises them. It says so quite clearly there, that that is the department of defence, and the appointments are made by the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna at the proposal of the head of the defence department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you a similar question, and you don't have to give us a long explanation. I'd just like to know a "yes" or "no" answer. This was a question asked by Mr. Nobilo on page 28, lines 14, and your answer which I will quote, part of it goes through line 22: "Could you tell us, please --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Last question. Otherwise, for the first time since this has started, I'm going to use this instrument. Last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Could you tell us, please, who decides on whether an investigation will be set into motion which represents the first step in a formal procedure? Who decides this, and Blaskic, as the commander of the Operative Zone, was he able to say that a procedure of this kind would be set in motion or not?" And your answer was, "No. This is the exclusive right of the investigative judge ..." and your answer goes on. When you gave that answer to that question, you, again, were not referring to the military disciplinary courts, were you?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not about disciplinary courts, about military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Seeing that I have run my time, Mr. President, I will not ask any additional questions. Mr. Tadic, I appreciate your answering my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Harmon, for having been so directive, but you took 20 minutes more than we had planned. You know, for the final arguments, we're not going to limit the time at all, nor will we do that for the Defence. About how much time do you need, Mr. Nobilo, because I'm really beginning to try to take some precautions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: As usual, very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, you didn't quite answer my question, but all right, go ahead. Re-examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, war crimes, crimes against humanity, is this a crime or is this a disciplinary offence?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course, it is a crime of the most serious kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Routinely speaking, in Bosnia, if someone were to commit a serious, important crime and, alongside it, made a traffic violation or some other minor offence, would he be tried for murder and for the traffic offence or if he had passed by a red light at the traffic lights, he would be tried for a criminal act? Now, I apologise for having to ask you in this way, but you are a witness in this case, so I apologise, but do you know the principle that subsumes -- that the more important act subsumes the lesser offence? I will repeat it once again because it was not introduced into the transcript. I apologise for having to ask you that question, for having to ask you basic facts relating to the law. I am asking you whether a more serious crime subsumes a lesser offence?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The more serious offence subsumes the lesser offence, and there is a clear-cut provision for this in the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in disciplinary measures and procedure, if the perpetrator is not known and we want to determine who the perpetrator is, not to improvise at this point, but when it is not clear immediately who has committed a disciplinary offence, who will investigate, the military police?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the military police will before it has reached the disciplinary prosecutor, and, of course, it won't reach that individual if the perpetrator is unknown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us return for a moment to something asked of you yesterday by the Prosecutor and Article 27 of the regulations governing military courts, where only mention is made of the commander of the Operative Zone; therefore, they are cases where the commander can detain the perpetrator of a criminal offence and must cooperate with the military police and keep all the evidence. In the spirit of that regulation and in the entirety of the regulations governing criminal acts and the law on criminal courts, is this a routine matter or is that an exception provided for for certain extreme cases?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Regular business of uncovering crimes and reporting them, reporting criminal acts, is usually done by the crime investigation department of the military police. This, therefore, is an exception, shall we say, because of the overall situation and the state of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give us an example. When could this provision be applied, in your opinion? For which cases is this provision, that is to say, Article 27 on the regulations governing military courts?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that I have quoted examples already. If the military police is not there and something has happened within a military unit, then the commander will undertake everything to detain that individual, to retain the evidence and traces, and to turn that individual over to the investigative judge and the military prosecutor. And if the military police arrives there before that, then it can take the case over into its own hands, and everything will evolve, according to the law, after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in the Law on Criminal Procedure, do the same competencies exist for every citizen, that is to say, that they can arrest a criminal and detain him until the police arrive?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The Law on Criminal Procedure does have a provision which states that citizens have the right when they come across and are on the spot where a crime has been committed, that they can detain that individual and inform the nearest police station of these occurrences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From all your knowledge, and especially your knowledge on the Law on Criminal Procedure and the regulations governing the military police that we have mentioned, tell us, please, whether a commander, the commander of the Operative Zone, has the duty to, himself, seek for the perpetrators of a crime and search for them or is this regulated in some other way?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First and foremost, the regulation relating to district military courts, as well as the Law on Criminal Procedure and its application in a war situation, it is stipulated that all the competencies that the regular police force has are taken over by the military police in wartime, that is to say, the service of the military police which means the criminal investigation police. And here, first and foremost, it is the task and role of the specialised, so to speak, services for matters of this kind, that is to say, the crime departments of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we move on to the next area. You saw an order, not signed by Blaskic, but it was an order nonetheless, from which it stems that Blaskic orders that if a unit or individual flees from the battleground, that the whole unit be executed or individual soldiers. Could you tell the Court now, please, whether, according to your knowledge, in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, there were instances where soldiers fled from the battleground?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean from the Croatian Defence Council as a military component, not the Croatian Community, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, fleeing from military units.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there were cases of this kind, just as there were in any other army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bosnia is not a big country, and the territory called the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is even a smaller territory. Have you ever heard of anybody being executed for fleeing from the battleground?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I've never heard of any cases of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you a hypothetical question. Perhaps it is not overly hypothetical, but for the purposes of your testimony, it is. If a unit of the military police, without the knowledge of the commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia and without his authorisation, sets fire to a village, kills 100 people, most of them civilians, and gives false information to the commander of what is going on when it is actually occurring, would this be a routine criminal procedure of the crime police or would it be a serious, enormous security problem for the enclave of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Quite certainly, it will be a very serious problem, and if that is something that the -- if the military police did do this, then other mechanisms should be sought, if I may say that, or other services should we sought to meritoriously be able to investigate this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which service, in your general knowledge, because you said you had no expert knowledge as regards the army, what service is authorised to investigate security matters, the security situation within the army?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is the service that we call SIS, the Security and Information Service, and its abbreviation was SIS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So SIS is the Security and Information Service?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was called SIS for short.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If this hypothesis were to be correct, the one that I have just put to you, would the order for an investigation into Ahmici given to SIS be valid nonetheless, in the sense of its official formal qualities?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that it would be logical to ask SIS to step in in a situation of this kind. If, therefore, the military police did something of that kind, then it is logical that it created an enormous problem, and it is the security service which would have to investigate and to be activated in that regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to go through the documents, I know your plane is due to leave shortly, but I will say, taking them all together, the last document was document 373, Defence Exhibit 373, where Tihomir Blaskic, as the commander ordered the warden of the military prison and all the brigade commanders and asked them to respect the Geneva Conventions with regard to prisoners of war. You said that he did not have that authorisation. Tell us now, please, as a legal man and from your overall knowledge, how do you assess Blaskic's actions which supersede his authorisations in order to ensure respect for the Geneva Conventions and the other qualitative matters, that is to say, his orders in that regard? How do you assess his conduct, taking everything into account?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I should like to ask Your Honours to understand the following: When I say something, I always look at the norms, the rules, regulations, and how they comply with other superior norms or acts, and in that sense, I said hierarchially what the situation should have been like. As a human being, as an individual, I understand and find it normal that a commander should pay care and attention to the fact that the Geneva Conventions are respected or not. Whether he did this in the right way by going through the courts to the prisons and the defence department, that is another matter because the defence department had supervision. But at all events, it would be affirmative and positive that he did pay care and attention to ensuring that the Geneva Conventions were respected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, in the case of conflict, under wartime conditions, I'm not talking about peacetime when the rule of law prevails, the conflict between formal law and implementing justice, what would you choose?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, formally speaking, legal men are always a little formalistic and must adhere to a certain amount of form, officialese, the judgment will fall through if the council and panel has not been set up as they should have been and if the court proceedings have not been as they should have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we're talking about Blaskic and his acts?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Here, we are faced with a situation of war. They are extraordinary situations, and they dictated -- it was the situation on the spot, on the terrain, which dictated matters, and I don't know whether I, as a legal man, had I found myself in a situation of this kind, would have acted in a different manner to what Mr. Blaskic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You were right, Mr. Nobilo. You didn't take much time. I know that we have to release Mr. Tadic. It's break time now. Let me first turn, however, to Judge Shahabuddeen and ask him whether he has any questions or would he prefer to do it afterwards? We're going to take a 20-minute break before moving to the Judges' questions because, in any case, you missed your plane, Mr. Tadic. So we're going to do our best to make sure you don't miss the next plane. We'll take a 20-minute break, and then we'll come back for the Judges' questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: May we continue. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen, would you like to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I do hope that any questions which I or my colleague may have for you will not unduly delay you and will enable you to catch your plane. I understand the imperatives which are involved. So I will ask you only a very few questions. My recollection is that you were appointed Justice Minister on 6th January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No. Then would you tell me what was the date?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The 6th of January, that's correct, the 6th of January, 1993 I was appointed assistant, assistant head of the department for justice and administration of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. So that is a big difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Herceg-Bosna. I see. I see. I appreciate the correction. Should I understand, then, that that appointment meant that you had no constitutional relationship to the government in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, the constitutional court in Sarajevo gave a decision on the 18th of September, 1992 in which it, effectively, declared itself to be annulling the establishment of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said yesterday that I am aware of such a decision, but I have never seen it. I have never read it. I got out of Sarajevo on the 28th of April, 1992, and all communications with Sarajevo were cut off, so there was no possibility of communicating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Tell me a little bit more about the exact constitutional relationship of Herceg-Bosna with the government in Sarajevo as the matter was seen by Herceg-Bosna. Herceg-Bosna, I believe, described itself as a component part of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether I am competent to give an answer of proper quality to your question, because this was part of politics, really, and I was not involved in that particular part. It is true that the Croatian community, I emphasize the Croatian community, not the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, pointed out that it was a component within the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On all documents it said the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and underneath that the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. Since I was away, I was in the north, what kind of communications there were between the political leadership on the one hand and Sarajevo on the other hand, I cannot give you a proper answer, qualified answer to that. When I was in Bosanska Posavina, that is in the north of Bosnia, I used to go to Zagreb, and part of the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was there. They were detached. They left Sarajevo and they were staying in Zagreb, in Senoina Street, and I communicated with them in relation to the establishment of the judiciary in Bosanska Posavina, because all communications with Sarajevo were cut off. However, this part of the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zagreb ceased to operate soon. This went on only for a few months. After that, it ceased to operate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I don't want to delay matters too much, so may I ask you this kind of question: As seen from the point of view of the Croatian community in Herceg-Bosna, was there still a constitutional relationship of some kind between that community and the government in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: With your permission -- I am sorry, my apologies. In Article 2 of the decree on military -- district military courts it says that they pass judgments on the basis of the constitution and laws. The Croatian community did not have a constitution. The constitution referred to was the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So should I take it that a decision of the constitutional court in Sarajevo had some significance or importance to a distinguished legal officer of your standing in the service of the community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We applied practically all the regulations of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were taken over by the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but, in all fairness, by the presidency of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna too. You will see in the decree on the Law on Criminal Procedure and the Criminal Code that there are only two articles, one which says that that Criminal Code and Law on Criminal Procedure are being taken over that were taken over by the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is quoted. There is another article saying that it enters into force immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could learn to abbreviate the proceedings in the interest of your own early departure. And then I would beg to remind you that my question was whether the decision of the constitutional court was perceived by someone in your position as having any importance or significance.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You don't know. I take your answer --

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know because I didn't see the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would it have been possible for you to see the decision if you had wanted, though?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: To be quite frank with you, I was not aware of its existence for quite some time, because there was a war going on and one had to save one's very life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, let us move away from the question of constitutionality to the question of the relationship between the Ministry of Defence and Colonel Blaskic. Now and then in the course of your testimony you said something to the effect that Colonel Blaskic would have been overstepping his authority.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, did the Ministry of Defence take any corrective action against Colonel Blaskic in respect of any acts by which he overstepped his authority?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, prosecuting counsel has shown you one or two documents addressed by Colonel Blaskic to the military police, in effect ordering them to take or to institute certain disciplinary procedures. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, did the military police ever object to the competence of Colonel Blaskic to issue such directives to the military police?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did Colonel Blaskic have someone in the position of a legal adviser to tell him when he was overstepping his authority?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know all these persons who worked with Colonel Blaskic. I do not know what they were by training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Prosecutor showed you certain disciplinary regulations promulgated by Mr. Mate Boban dated 3rd of July, 1992. I think you said this was the first time you were seeing them. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, I would like to collect or write your exact position on these regulations. Should I understand you to mean that this is the first time you were seeing the regulations, but you are not doubting the authenticity of the regulations?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do you accept the authenticity of the regulations, but are you saying this is the first time you've seen them?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that until now I had not studied or read these regulations. I am not denying its authenticity. I am not saying that it's forged or something like that. So I have not read it, because I never needed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you a general question like this. The laws have many objectives, but, basically, in relation to situations am I right that they may do these things: They may call into being a new situation or they may prohibit the continuance of an existing situation or they may accept that an existing situation is inevitable and seek to regulate it? Would you respond to that synopsis? Do you think that's a fair analysis of the functions of law?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly. Laws are supposed to regulate a certain situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you say whether the laws of Herceg-Bosna would have recognised the inevitability of a situation in which a battlefield commander has to have a certain measure of disciplinary authority if he is to wield his competence effectively?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The laws attempted to resolve the situation in terms of what it should be under new circumstances, that is to say in a state of war, and in that sense there were interventions in certain laws in order to have them adjusted to the war situation. For example, in the Law on Criminal Procedure, the periods for appeal were considerably shortened, the composition of panels of judges were changed, et cetera, and other steps were taken in order to make work more operative, so-to-speak. Disciplinary action which was within the authority of the military, that is to say of the commander, he would regulate the situation in his own way. So, certainly attempts were made through this law to adjust to the given situation, but invariably, bearing in mind the law and observance of the law as things were in civilian life or, rather, in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I hope you do catch your plane. I thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you too, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen. I will try to be sure that you can take your plane. I would like to thank Judge Shahabuddeen for having asked some questions that go to the very heart of our discussions. Am I wrong when I say that your functions put you at the meeting point between problems of justice, military justice, and all of this in wartime in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is not the best possible interpretation. I was not within the system of military justice. I was assistant head of the department of justice and administration. It was a kind of secretariat which had its chief. I was not the chief. I was one of the three assistant chiefs. My task was to establish in the Posavina the civilian judiciary and the military judiciary. That's what I did. And in March, 1993, in Posavina, in Bosanska Posavina, the civilian and military judiciary started to operate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But can we say that the structures of military justice for the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, were you very involved in working on them, in drafting them? Did you supervise them? We are talking specifically about military justice.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Supervision over military justice and the military prosecutors office was exercised by the Department of Defence. Now, what did we do? We tried to provide the necessary persons, that is to say judges, prosecutors, and then material that was needed for work, registers, typewriters, offices, everything that was needed so that they would start working. Because they used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, all of the logistics.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Part of the logistics involved. Part of the logistics involved. We did not provide for their salaries. It was the defence department that did that. And the defence department provided for salaries and for the rest of logistics, but we provided for part of logistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But as regards the constitutive text for military justice, did you have meetings, did you give advice in which it would give the opinion of the Ministry of Justice about the text that had been set up by the ministry of --

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, perhaps as a legal specialist you can clarify the treatment in the Yugoslav Criminal Code about genocide and war crimes. Ordinarily, did the Yugoslav Code provide for punishment for war crimes? I suppose it continues to punish them.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes. These are the gravest crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The question I wanted to ask you is the following: In your opinion, like in all armies in the world, in war time, a commander in an Operative Zone, as like the accused, does the commander have powers to denounce people, to carry out investigations and to defer cases to the military courts? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No. He could report people, but not order custody against them, except in Article 27, in cases mentioned in Article 27, when a known perpetrator is involved or, rather, when this happened in his unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I didn't get the interpretation. Do you have anything you could tell us about what one teaches military officers at the military academy in respect of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As part of your work, were you in contact with the political leaders of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From time to time, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Did you know their political plans as regards the constitution of that community?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established before I came to join its structures. I have to emphasise that Bosanska Posavina was not immediately part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This was some time at the end of 1992, October, November, I'm not quite sure when. So the Croatian Community already existed when I joined its structures. And as regards further plans, I did not take part in that. I tried to only see to my professional duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you agree with me when I say that in all the armies of the world, the rules of military discipline are known, that is, that you have to punish the operational commander, a general, for 60 days, that is, he can arrest people and hold them for 60 days? But do you agree with me when I say that is not what the problem is? That's not the question. We all know that General Blaskic had powers against somebody who would not salute him in the morning. That's common in all armies of the world when it comes to military discipline, that is, you can be arrested if you don't do what you're supposed to do. I suppose that you did military service, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So did I. So did I.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But that's not the problem here. The problem is that this is wartime. There was a political project of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So my question is, as regards this entire structure of military organisation, was it intended more to seat Colonel Blaskic's power over his troops or, at the same time, did it also give him the power to punish failures, serious failures, to respect the laws of war, crimes that might have been committed? It seems to me that that is the real question. That is what I think.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I understood your question, did he have powers to punish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. Could we say that this entire architecture of texts the Prosecutor showed to us, could we say that, in your opinion, these texts were designed only in order to seat the hierarchical authority of the accused in respect of all of the military structures that came under him, that is, in respect of discipline, for example, as everybody knows, or would we say that these same legal instruments, did they give him the power to prosecute and to investigate war crimes, genocide, crimes against humanity, committed under his authority? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I think specifically when I saw these documents, that this is a question of authority of the commander who is supposed to build this kind of authority among his troops because these were special circumstances. And sometimes he does overstep his authority in order to keep discipline and his authority because this is not a professional army. This was an army that was only in the making, that was in its very inception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, my question is whether the legal structures that, in wartime, the commander of the Operations Zone had, could he use that power?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, he was not given such powers. He was given powers up to a certain extent, and those were his powers, and the rest was supposed to be carried out by other structures, and that could be seen from the regulations too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I thought that that's what your answer would be. My last question is in another area. If I've understood what you said, I still have somewhat of an impression that when serious crimes, not little failures to obey military discipline, when those kind of crimes, serious ones, are committed, when he was involved with them, he was not supposed to because he was overstepping his authority, and when he did take care and when he was in Ahmici, then that was the greatness of soul which led the accused to do so. You, who are a legal specialist, are saying that there is no legal specific instrument. So my question is, do you think that in any army in the world, at least the civilised world, wouldn't you think that there are legal instruments?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have not had the opportunity to see other regulations. It is quite understandable to me that this should be regulated. Every crime should be investigated and punished. In this specific case, whether, strictly formally speaking, he acted accordingly or not, that is a different question because our Law on Criminal Procedure had a certain procedure involved, one that was envisaged in the law. In practice, there were certain dilemmas as regards its implementation, and this was the case here too in a few instances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In other words, either we're talking about minor discipline, which is not the proper case here, or else we're dealing with very serious issues, and it's through the goodwill on the part of the accused, that is, generals, not only him, but that there was an entire field which had not been provided for. So I go back to what Judge Shahabuddeen said. Were there legal specialists?
